**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity (e.g. your name, school, parentage etc). You should write between 450 - 500 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **g)** Why do candidates perform poorly in examinations? What measures can be taken to remedy the situation?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: poor results worry everybody.
2. Causes: lack of preparation, shortage of teachers and materials, malpractice, poverty, weak examination technique.
3. Measures by students and parents.
4. Measures by the government and schools.
5. Conclusion.

**Model composition (460 words)**

Every year, thousands of candidates sit for public examinations in Cameroon, and every year the results show that a large number of them fail. This poor performance worries parents, teachers and the government, and it wastes the money and effort invested in education. In my view, there are several causes, but there are also practical measures that can improve the situation.

One major cause is lack of serious preparation. Many candidates waste time on telephones, social media, films and football instead of studying. They start revising only a few weeks before the examination, and they depend on guesswork and "tips" rather than on a full understanding of the syllabus. Others read only the night before and, being tired, forget most of what they have learnt.

Another cause is the shortage of qualified teachers and teaching materials. In many schools, particularly in rural areas, classes are overcrowded, laboratories are empty and textbooks are scarce. Teachers who are poorly paid may be absent or unmotivated, and some subjects are not taught at all for months. Candidates in such schools cannot be expected to do well in practical subjects.

A third cause is examination malpractice. Some students believe that they can pass by copying or by buying answers, so they do not bother to work. When they find themselves in a well-supervised hall, they panic and fail. Poverty also plays a part: a child who comes to school hungry, or who is sent home for unpaid fees, cannot concentrate. Finally, many candidates lack examination technique; they misread the questions, manage their time badly or write answers that are too short and unclear.

Fortunately, these problems can be solved. First, students must draw up a timetable and study regularly from the beginning of the year, with time for rest. They should practise past questions, form discussion groups and ask teachers for help where they do not understand. Parents must also supervise the work of their children, limit their use of phones and provide a quiet place to study at home.

Secondly, the government should recruit and train more teachers, pay them promptly and provide libraries, laboratories and enough textbooks to every school. School authorities, for their part, should organise regular tests and remedial classes for weak students. Thirdly, strict supervision must be maintained during examinations, and cheaters should be punished firmly so that nobody expects to succeed by dishonest means. Guidance and counselling services can also teach candidates how to manage time, handle stress and answer questions correctly.

In conclusion, poor performance in examinations is caused by laziness, poor teaching conditions, malpractice, poverty and weak examination technique. If students, parents, teachers and the government play their part, results will improve, and our candidates will be proud of their success and ready for the future.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Answering only one of the two questions (the causes OR the remedies); both must be developed.
2. Blaming one group only (for example only the students), with no measures matched to each cause.
